title: Bailey sets out four ways an AI investment success could still disappoint investors
summary: Andrew Bailey’s opening remarks in Zurich separate two questions often conflated when markets price a new technology. Artificial intelligence may lift the economy’s sustainable growth rate, while the securities funding that investment can still be overpriced. The Governor points to business services and AI-related investment as part of the reason UK activity has been more resilient than expected. He offers no numerical estimate of the productivity gain, a fair valuation for technology companies or a view on the next Bank Rate decision. The substance is a framework for recognising risks to financial stability while allowing productive investment to develop.

The immediate backdrop is a combination of adverse supply shocks from conflicts in Europe and the Middle East and a potentially favourable supply shock from new technology. The former can raise inflation while lowering output, making the trade-off facing the central bank more difficult. Investment in AI can contribute to current activity before the long-term productive capacity it might deliver can be measured. A researcher should therefore distinguish stronger demand for equipment and services today from a sufficiently durable rise in potential output to justify higher future cash flows. Bailey also notes Switzerland’s more subdued inflation history in addressing a Zurich audience. The same external shock need not produce the same domestic inflation profile. In the UK evidence Bailey cited, business services stood out. He attributed part of the upside in activity to AI investment there. He offered no sectoral estimate of productivity or of how much of the spending would ultimately translate into higher sustainable growth.

Bailey’s defence of independence is linked to this uncertainty. Institutions must be able to restore price stability when the alternative uses of policy are contested, but their legitimacy rests on serving and answering to the whole population. His description of financial regulation is more politically contentious than his description of independent interest-rate decisions. The constituencies directly affected by a rule are identifiable, lobbying is more intense and memories of the financial crisis have receded. For investors assessing a call to loosen regulation, he proposes an awkward counterfactual: the resilience of the system through recent shocks may reflect the measures now under pressure to be removed. It cannot establish that those measures had become unnecessary. He accepts that individual UK rules may deserve change and observes that risk has moved to new parts of the system.

The first of his four valuation risks is straightforward overestimation of the eventual returns from AI. The second is a timing mismatch: investment can produce the returns originally envisaged, but only after cash flows have been discounted for longer or financing has to be rolled over. His historical analogy is the time it took electricity to generate its full economic benefits. That risk is especially relevant when firms make large initial commitments and their counterparties depend on sufficiently rapid take-up. The third is an aggregation problem. Market prices can embody successful outcomes for many competing firms even though some must lose market share. Netscape illustrates how a transformative technology need not reward each early participant. Testing the industry’s total revenue opportunity and testing whether each issuer can earn its implied share are separate exercises.

The fourth route runs through public trust. A failure that undermines confidence could delay adoption and alter expected revenue, without disproving the underlying technology. Bailey links trust to model testing before and after deployment, human intervention, incident reporting and follow-up. Operational vulnerabilities also matter to institutions that rely on AI. The proposed safeguards are relevant to markets insofar as they affect adoption, the reliability of critical activities or liabilities after a failure. The speech provides no evidence that a particular loss has already occurred and offers no numerical estimates of the affected exposures.

For macro research, the distinction between equity losses and an impairment to the financial system is consequential. A lower valuation borne by diversified equity holders is different from a funding interruption that forces firms to stop investing or lenders to liquidate collateral. Bailey identifies possible reasons for disappointing market valuations, but does not map who owns the risk, the maturity of liabilities or what would trigger forced sales. Those missing inputs define the test of a systemic scenario. A fall in prices could reflect overly optimistic earnings, delayed adoption, lost market share or a trust event. The operating and financing evidence required to discriminate among them differs. This is a Governor’s institutional and financial-stability argument. Turning it into a directional Bank Rate signal would discard the questions he actually addresses.

questions.question: Could adoption succeed on the original scale but arrive too late for current financing structures?
questions.detail: Compare the original commissioning schedule, contracted demand, debt maturities and funding covenants with realised capacity utilisation. Delay with intact eventual demand implies lower present value and potentially greater refinancing needs; weaker eventual demand reduces the expected amount of cash received. If debt matures well after cash generation and the investment is predominantly equity financed, the financial-stability channel is less compelling even if equity prices fall.

questions.question: Does the market’s expected profit pool require an implausible number of winners?
questions.detail: Aggregate the capacity and revenue assumptions implicit in individual firms’ forecasts, accounting for transactions among suppliers and customers to avoid counting the same sale twice. Compare the resulting industry total with demand from final users and investigate market-share assumptions among close substitutes. Disappointment concentrated among competitors would fit redistribution of an otherwise viable technology. Simultaneous reductions in end-user demand would suggest a different aggregate risk.

questions.question: Which event would turn a loss of public trust into a macro-financial shock?
questions.detail: Specify the sequence before examining outcomes: a documented incident, a measurable reduction in adoption or interruption to a critical service, and a financing or liquidity exposure large enough to transmit the loss. Compare affected users with otherwise similar firms that have alternative providers or effective human intervention. A valuation adjustment without evidence of lower activity, impaired intermediation or widespread operational dependence would be weaker support for a systemic interpretation.

limitation: The publication contains the Governor’s opening remarks. It offers a qualitative assessment of independent institutions, investment and financial stability, without a quantified stress test, an MPC vote or a proposed rate path.
